Short random walks stay trapped inside each cluster, so Walktrap returns the two clusters as communities, drawn as tinted regions in teal and the accent color. The card lists community 0 as D, E, F, G and community 1 as A, B, C." width="100%"} The Walktrap algorithm exploits the property that random walks tend to stay trapped within densely connected communities. It computes distances between nodes based on random walk probabilities, then uses hierarchical clustering to identify community structure. Works only with undirected graphs. On a disconnected graph each connected component is clustered separately, so a community never spans two components and an isolated node is a community of its own. Time complexity is `O(n²log n)` for typical networks with small step parameter. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [steps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[4]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of random walk steps. Higher values capture longer-range structural patterns. Typical values: 2-8. - steps=2: Local structure only - steps=4: Good balance (default, recommended) - steps=6+: Longer-range patterns, more computation [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store community assignments in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `cmty_walktrap`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to community IDs (0-indexed, contiguous). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Walktrap (Pons and Latapy, 2005) rests on a simple observation: a random walk on a graph tends to get *trapped* inside densely connected regions before escaping through sparse bridges. The algorithm builds the $t$-step transition matrix $P^t$ from the row-stochastic $P_{ij} = 1/\deg(i)$, defines a random-walk distance $d(i, j) = \sqrt{\sum_k \dfrac{(P^t_{ik} - P^t_{jk})^2}{\deg(k)}}$ that grows small whenever two nodes send walks to similar destinations, then feeds those distances into Ward's agglomerative hierarchical clustering. The dendrogram is finally cut at the level of maximum modularity. Small `steps` values (2 or 3) surface fine-grained local communities; larger values (5 to 8) reveal coarser structure. Nothing about the procedure is random despite the name, and the $O(n^2)$ distance matrix is the practical scaling ceiling around $10\,000$ nodes. Self-loops and multi-edges are not currently supported. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Random walks starting inside either triangle tend to stay there, since crossing the bridge is comparatively rare -- so Walktrap recovers the same two communities: ::: {#d3eff330 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) # Two cliques connected by a bridge graph.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D"), ("C", "D")]) # Bridge communities = graph.cmty_walktrap(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): cid for nid, cid in communities.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'C': 0, 'A': 0, 'E': 1, 'F': 1, 'D': 1, 'B': 0} ``` ::: ::: Fewer `steps` favors detecting finer, more local structure, while more `steps` looks at longer-range patterns -- on a graph this small, both settings still land on the same two communities: ::: {#cd74b969 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} local_cmty = graph.cmty_walktrap(return_dict=True, steps=2) global_cmty = graph.cmty_walktrap(return_dict=True, steps=6) len(set(local_cmty.values())), len(set(global_cmty.values())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (2, 2) ``` ::: ::: Storing the result as a node attribute and chaining into `colorize_node_attrs()` visualizes the communities directly: ::: {#88dca7a1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")]) ) ( graph .cmty_walktrap(attr_name="community") .colorize_node_attrs(node_attr_from="community", palette="tableau") .describe() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of nodes : 6 Number of edges : 7 Directed : False Density : 0.47 Average degree (min, max) : 2.33 (2, 3) Connected : True Number of connected components : 1 Tree : False Bipartite : False Computations: - cmty_walktrap() -> attr: 'community' (6 of 6 nodes) Node aesthetics: - color <- community via colorize (palette: "tableau") (values: #4e79a7, #f28e2c, 6 of 6 nodes) ``` ::: :::
